documentTitle: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
documentDescription: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
content:
Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines static and dynamic rendering in a single route. At build time, Next.js generates a static HTML shell and a postponedState blob for each PPR-enabled route. At request time, the shell is served immediately and dynamic portions are rendered and streamed to the client.

This page explains how platforms can implement PPR support at different levels of sophistication.

documentTitle: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
documentDescription: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
content:
For each PPR route, Next.js produces:

A static HTML shell containing all the content that can be prerendered, with Suspense fallbacks where dynamic content will appear.A postponedState value: a serialized string. Treat it as opaque: pass it through without parsing or modifying it. Altering postponedState produces incorrect dynamic rendering output.An RSC payload for the static portions of the page.

documentTitle: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
documentDescription: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
content:
When a request arrives for a PPR route:

The server sends the static HTML shell to the client immediately.The server resumes rendering the dynamic portions using the postponed state.Dynamic content is streamed to the client, allowing React to hydrate the deferred Suspense boundaries.

The client sees the static shell instantly, then dynamic content appears as it resolves.

documentTitle: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
documentDescription: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
content:
Each PPR route requires two artifacts to be stored together:

The static HTML shell.The postponedState blob.

These must be stored and updated atomically. When a PPR route is revalidated (via time-based or on-demand revalidation), Next.js regenerates both the shell and the postponed state together. Serving a new shell with an old postponed state, or vice versa, will produce incorrect dynamic content.

Use requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2 in your adapter to observe cache updates and propagate them to your storage backend.

documentTitle: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
documentDescription: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
content:
This is the simplest approach and works on every platform that supports streaming HTTP responses.

All requests go directly to the Next.js server. The server reads the shell from its local cache, sends it, then renders and streams the dynamic content. This is what next start does by default.

No additional infrastructure is needed. If your platform supports streaming HTTP responses, it supports PPR.

documentTitle: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
documentDescription: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
content:
For better TTFB, the static HTML shell can be cached at the CDN edge. When a request arrives:

The CDN serves the cached shell immediately (edge latency).The CDN sends a resume request to the origin server (ideally in parallel with streaming the shell).The origin server renders only the dynamic portions and streams them back.The CDN concatenates the shell and dynamic content into a single streaming response to the client.

This requires the CDN to support a mechanism for combining cached and dynamic content in a single streaming response. The static shell TTFB drops to edge latency while dynamic content still streams from origin.

For the lowest possible latency, the shell can be served from edge storage (for example, a KV store populated during onBuildComplete) rather than from a CDN cache. This is a platform architecture decision and does not require any changes to the Next.js application.

content:
The resume protocol tells the Next.js handler to skip the shell and render only the dynamic portions. It is used by CDN-to-origin architectures and adapter-based deployments that serve the shell separately.

In standard next start, the server handles both the shell and dynamic render in a single pass automatically.

documentTitle: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
documentDescription: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
content:
When the CDN makes an HTTP request to a separate Next.js origin:

Send a POST request to the route with the header next-resume: 1.Include the postponedState blob as the request body.The server will render only the deferred Suspense boundaries and stream the result.

Good to know: When a POST request combines a Server Action with a PPR resume, the request body contains the postponed state followed by the action body. The x-next-resume-state-length header carries the byte length of the postponed state prefix so the handler can separate the two. For a pure PPR resume (the common case), the entire request body is the postponed state and this header is not needed.

documentTitle: Implementing Partial Prerendering on your platform
documentDescription: A guide for platform engineers on implementing PPR support, from basic origin rendering to optimized CDN integration.
content:
When the platform invokes the handler function directly:

Call the entrypoint handler with req.method set to 'POST', the next-resume: 1 header on the request, and the postponedState as the request body. (You can also pass requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState } as the third argument to the handler invocation, which is equivalent but bypasses the HTTP layer entirely.)The handler renders only the deferred Suspense boundaries and streams the result to res.No HTTP round-trip is needed: the handler is invoked in-process.

sectionTitle: Finding PPR routes in build output
content:
In the adapter output, PPR routes are identified by renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC' in the prerenders array. Iterate outputs.prerenders to find these entries and read fallback.postponedState.

pprChain.headers contains the headers needed for the resume protocol: { 'next-resume': '1' }.

For detailed implementation with code examples, see Implementing PPR in an Adapter.

content: Read PPR outputs at build time. In your adapter's onBuildComplete, identify prerenders with renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'. Store the shell HTML and postponedState in your cache.Serve the shell at request time. For incoming requests to PPR routes, serve the cached shell immediately and begin streaming.Resume dynamic rendering. For CDN-to-origin: send a POST request to the Next.js handler with the next-resume: 1 header and the postponed state as the body. For adapter-based: call the handler directly with POST method and the postponed state in the request body (or pass requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState } to the handler). Stream the response back to the client.Handle cache updates. Use requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2 to capture new shell + postponed state pairs after revalidation, and update your cache atomically.Support graceful degradation.
